title: Rules and agreements exist
keyIdea: Rules are there for a reason. Some rules keep us safe. Some keep things fair. Some help us work together. With no rules, people get hurt, left out or muddled. An agreement is a rule a group makes together, and a good one works for everyone. Different places need different rules. We keep a rule because of its reason, so it still counts when nobody is watching.

kid: A rule tells us what to do. Every rule has a reason. Walk inside, so you do not trip. Take turns on the swing, so all get a go.
Think of a game of tag with no rules. Who is it? Who is out? Nobody knows! Rules make the game work. They help us play together.
An agreement is a rule we make together. Your class can agree: one talks, the rest listen. A good agreement makes every friend happy.
Each place has its own rules. Be quiet in the library, so people can read. Walk at the pool, as the floor is wet. Keep a rule even when no grown-up can see. The reason is still there.
adult: At this age children are learning that rules are not just orders from adults. Rules exist for reasons: to keep people safe, to make things fair, and to help a group work together. The PSHE Association programme of study asks Key Stage 1 pupils to learn what rules are, why they are needed, and why different rules are needed for different situations. The non-statutory KS1 citizenship framework asks them to agree and follow rules for their group and classroom, and to understand how rules help them.

A common mistake is to explain rules only as 'because I said so'. Children then tend to keep rules only while an adult is watching. When you name the reason, such as 'walk, because the floor is slippery', the rule makes sense on its own, and children are more likely to keep it when you step away. Asking 'what could happen if we had no rule here?' helps them work out the reason for themselves.

An agreement is a rule a group makes together, like a class charter. Children this age can judge a fair agreement by asking whether it works for everyone, not just the loudest or the oldest child. Another mistake is to think fair means 'I get my way'. Voting, taking turns to choose and listening while one person talks are agreements they can try at home with siblings or at a playdate.

In the lab your child sorts rules by their reason: safe, fair or together. They watch a slide, a hall and a game of tag fall into chaos with no rule, then drag in the rule that fixes each one. A grown-up looks away and they choose whether the rule still counts. They pick group agreements and see every face react, then match rules to the library, the pool and football. Every drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: Make one family agreement together this week, such as how screen time or bath time works. Let everyone say what they think, then write it down and stick it up. When someone forgets, ask 'what was our reason?' instead of just repeating the rule.

visual.caption: Why is this rule here? Drag each rule, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Hold hands to cross the road
Wear a helmet on your bike
Agree on a plan for the den

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort rules by reason, fix places with no rules, keep a rule when nobody looks, make fair agreements and match rules to places.

practice.prompt: Why do we walk, not run, inside?
choices: So nobody trips and gets hurt
Because running is too much fun
practice.hint: Think about what could happen if you ran.
practice.explain: We walk inside so nobody trips and gets hurt. That rule keeps us safe.

practice.prompt: {n} children want a go on the slide. Each child gets 1 go. How many goes in all?
practice.explain: {n} children with 1 go each make {=n} goes. Taking turns means every child gets a go.

practice.prompt: The teacher goes out of the room. Do the class rules still count?
choices: Yes, the reason is still there
practice.hint: Is the floor still slippery when she goes?
practice.explain: Yes, the rules still count. The reason for a rule does not go away when nobody is looking.

practice.prompt: A class has {n} rules. 1 rule is about being quiet. How many other rules are there?
practice.explain: {n} take away 1 is {=n-1}. Every one of those rules has a reason too.

pool.prompt: What would happen in a game of tag with no rules?
choices: Nobody would know who is out
It would be more fun for all
pool.hint: Think about who is it and who is out.
pool.explain: With no rules, nobody would know who is out, so the game would not work. Rules help us play together.

pool.prompt: Which is a fair agreement for choosing a game?
pool.hint: Fair means it works for everyone.
pool.explain: Taking turns to choose is fair, because everyone gets a go. The other two only work for one child.

pool.prompt: Why should you use a quiet voice in the library?
pool.hint: What are people doing in a library?
pool.explain: Use a quiet voice because people in the library are reading and thinking. The rule fits what happens there.

pool.prompt: Mum says one biscuit each, then goes upstairs. What do you do?
choices: Take one, so all get one
Take lots: she will not know
pool.hint: Think about what the rule is for: is it about being fair?
pool.explain: Take one, so everyone gets one. The rule is there to be fair, even when Mum cannot see.

pool.prompt: Running is fine in the park. Is it fine at the pool?
choices: No, the pool floor is wet
Yes, rules are the same everywhere
pool.hint: Think about the floor at a pool. Is it the same as grass?
pool.explain: No, because the pool floor is wet and slippery. Different places need different rules.

pool.hint: An agreement is made by a group.
pool.explain: The class makes it together. That is what makes it an agreement, and why it works for everyone.

pool.prompt: {n} friends make an agreement. All of them are happy but 1. How many are happy?
pool.explain: {n} take away 1 is {=n-1}. One friend is still sad, so try a fairer agreement.

pool.prompt: Why do we have a rule to hold hands crossing the road?
choices: To keep us safe from cars
pool.hint: Think about the cars on the road and what could happen.
pool.explain: Holding hands keeps us safe from cars. It is a safe rule.

pool.prompt: A fair rule: each of the {n} children gets 2 stickers. How many stickers is that?
pool.hint: Count 2 stickers for each child, then add them up.
pool.explain: {n} children with 2 stickers each is {=2*n} stickers. Everyone gets the same, so it is fair.
